name: Computerized information retrieval
definition: A machine that stores very large collections of records or documents and finds the items matching a query in seconds.
what: Web search engines such as Google, handling tens of millions of searches a day over a billion indexed pages in under half a second, became everyday tools by about 2000.
fit: Ordinary people routinely query a huge document collection and get matches in a fraction of a second.

sources.title: The W5YI Report
sources.quote: with more than a billion pages indexed which can be accessed in less than half a second

note: Earlier consumer online services (Dialog 1980s, CompuServe) were niche; date is approximate for 'became common'.

name: Question-answering computer
definition: A computer holding broad knowledge that answers arbitrary factual questions put to it in ordinary language.
what: MIT's START went online on the Internet in 1993 and answered English questions from the public on many topics (Boris Katz)
fit: A publicly reachable computer answering ordinary-language factual questions on many topics, used by outside people for that purpose; knowledge is hand-annotated so breadth is limited.

sources.title: Boris Katz
sources.quote: Boris Katz is the creator of the START information processing system (since 1993 - on the Internet)

note: Kept from the second pass. No earlier deployed open-domain question answerer was found (Protosynthex was a research system). Ask Jeeves 1996 is later and matched questions to pages. No contemporary 1993-1995 source found in ia_search3.

name: Question-answering computer
definition: A computer holding broad knowledge that answers arbitrary factual questions put to it in ordinary language.
what: Apple's Siri, integrated into the iPhone 4S at its release on 14 October 2011, put spoken question answering in millions of ordinary users' hands
fit: A consumer device that answers ordinary-language factual questions (e.g. how tall is Mount Everest) for everyday users; knowledge is drawn from web services such as Wikipedia.

sources.title: Siri
sources.quote: integrated it into the iPhone 4s at its release on October 14, 2011

note: Earlier: Ask Jeeves (1996) accepted natural-language questions but returned page links, not answers. Later: Alexa/Google Assistant 2014-2016. Date is a judgement of when answering by voice became routine.

name: Electronic book reader
definition: A portable screen device that displays the text of books and documents stored electronically in place of paper.
what: Sony released the Data Discman DD-1 in Japan: a postcard-size player that reads text from 3-inch CDs and shows it on a built-in LCD.
fit: A pocket-size battery device with its own LCD that shows the text of books and reference works stored on a 3-inch CD, replacing paper.

sources.title: Sony Data Discman
sources.quote: The DD-1 was the earlier Japanese model in 1990.

note: Replaces 1972 Yevick and Wally, for whom I found only a 1973 US patent notice (George J. Yevick, 'Mechanical optical scanner', Official Gazette 1973-05-22) and Wikipedia's unreferenced claim; a patent or concept is not a demonstration, and no working unit or contemporary report was found. Dynabook (Kay, 1968-72) was a concept only; Bob Brown's 1930 'Readies' a proposal; Michael Hart's 1971 e-texts needed a mainframe. Sony's Data Discman DD-1 was announced May 1990 (Japan Times index) and released in Japan in July 1990; it is a commercial product, so demonstration and first practical use are the same event. Not checked: earlier Japanese dictionary/electronic-book handhelds of the 1980s (Sharp, Casio) that held a single reference text.

name: Electronic book reader
definition: A portable screen device that displays the text of books and documents stored electronically in place of paper.
what: The same Sony Data Discman DD-1 went on sale in Japan in July 1990 as an 'electronic book' player for reference works.
fit: A pocket-size battery device with its own LCD that shows the text of books and reference works stored on a 3-inch CD, replacing paper.

sources.title: Sony Data Discman
sources.quote: The DD-1 was the earlier Japanese model in 1990.

note: Replaces 1972 Yevick and Wally, for whom I found only a 1973 US patent notice (George J. Yevick, 'Mechanical optical scanner', Official Gazette 1973-05-22) and Wikipedia's unreferenced claim; a patent or concept is not a demonstration, and no working unit or contemporary report was found. Dynabook (Kay, 1968-72) was a concept only; Bob Brown's 1930 'Readies' a proposal; Michael Hart's 1971 e-texts needed a mainframe. Sony's Data Discman DD-1 was announced May 1990 (Japan Times index) and released in Japan in July 1990; it is a commercial product, so demonstration and first practical use are the same event. Not checked: earlier Japanese dictionary/electronic-book handhelds of the 1980s (Sharp, Casio) that held a single reference text.

name: Electronic book reader
definition: A portable screen device that displays the text of books and documents stored electronically in place of paper.
what: Amazon reported that in Q2 2010 it sold more Kindle e-books than hardcover books, with Kindle, Nook and iPad readers common in the US by 2010-11.
fit: Ordinary readers routinely read books on portable screen devices (Kindle, Nook, iPad) instead of paper.

sources.title: E-book
sources.quote: sales of e-books for its proprietary Kindle, outnumbered sales of hardcover books for the first time ever during the second quarter of 2010

sources.title: E-reader
sources.quote: a device which, upon its release in 2007, sold out within five and a half hours

note: A judgement: the Kindle launched in Nov 2007 and sold out in 5.5 hours, but e-books outselling hardcovers (2010) and passing paperbacks at Amazon (Jan 2011) marks routine use. Earlier e-readers (Rocket eBook, SoftBook 1998) did not gain widespread acceptance.

name: Three-dimensional holographic display
definition: A display that shows images, maps or people as volumetric three-dimensional pictures viewable from several sides.
what: The Actuality Systems Perspecta Spatial 3D volumetric display was integrated with a clinical radiation-therapy planning system (Pinnacle) so that planners could view patient anatomy and beams in 3D from any side.
fit: A swept-volume display showing changing patient-derived 3-D images in a 25 cm volume viewable from any side, used for its real purpose in treatment planning.

sources.publisher: Journal of Applied Clinical Medical Physics (PMC)
sources.title: Application of a 3D volumetric display for radiation therapy treatment planning I: quality assurance procedures
sources.quote: volume that is viewable from any side, floating within a translucent dome

sources.publisher: Journal of Applied Clinical Medical Physics (PMC)
sources.title: Application of a 3D volumetric display for radiation therapy treatment planning I: quality assurance procedures
sources.quote: has been integrated with the Pinnacle TPS (Philips Medical Systems, Madison WI), for treatment planning

note: Replaces second pass 1972 (Cross's moving multiplex hologram, an art/exhibit piece). The date is that of the clinical paper; a web search suggests the first Perspecta was delivered to the NIH Clinical Center in January 2004 (AuntMinnie, host blocked) and 2002 sales to universities for research, so real use probably began about 2002-2004, but I could not fetch a dated source. No earlier use outside the lab found for ITT's 1960 rotating-screen display (only a working model) or Withey's Peritron. Zebra Imaging's printed holographic maps for the US military are static, so excluded.

name: Computer screen display
definition: A screen on which a computer shows text, graphics or data to its user, in place of printouts or dials.
what: Home and office microcomputers with built-in or attached video screens (Apple II, TRS-80, PET, then the IBM PC) reached ordinary households and offices; Time named the computer its 'Man of the Year' for 1982.
fit: Ordinary people routinely read text and graphics from a computer on a screen at work, school and home.

sources.title: Time 1983-01-03
sources.quote: TIME's Man of the Year for 1982 is not a man but the computer itself

sources.title: Home computer
sources.quote: Home computers were a class of microcomputers that entered the market in 1977 and became common during the 1980s.

note: The year is a judgement: screens on computers entered homes in 1977 and became common in the early-to-mid 1980s (estimated 621,000 home computers in US households in 1982 per Wikipedia); video terminals were routine for office workers in the 1970s. Not a measured threshold.

name: Real-time computerized situation display
definition: A computer-driven screen or plotting board that shows the live positions of ships, aircraft or objects tracked by radar and sensors.
what: Public live flight-tracking displays (Flightradar24, opened to contributors in 2009, iOS and Android apps in 2010) let ordinary people watch real aircraft positions on screens; the 2010 Icelandic ash disruption made them widely used.
fit: A computer screen shows the live positions of aircraft tracked by ground receivers (ADS-B transponder signals, i.e. sensors rather than primary radar), available to anyone.

sources.title: Flightradar24
sources.quote: The service received extensive exposure in 2010, when international media relied on it to describe the flight disruption over the North Atlantic and Europe

note: No second-pass mass adoption. Judgment: the definition's military wording suggests none, but ordinary-people use of live tracked-position displays begins with public flight trackers (FlightAware 2005, Flightradar24 2009-10) or earlier GPS vehicle maps; I chose 2010 from the one fetched source. Looser than the definition (ADS-B, not radar).

name: Touchscreen and gesture interface
definition: Controlling a machine by touching a screen or panel, or by hand gestures and gloves read by sensors.
what: E. A. Johnson (Royal Radar Establishment, Malvern) published a finger-driven capacitive touch display for computer input/output (air traffic control) in Electronics Letters
fit: A transparent capacitive screen over a display let a user control a computer by touching the screen with a finger, matching the touch-screen mechanism.

sources.title: Touch display - a novel input/output device for computers
sources.quote: Touch display—a novel input/output device for computers

sources.title: Touchscreen
sources.quote: He described his work on capacitive touchscreens in a short article published in 1965

note: Confirms the second pass, now with a contemporary source (Crossref record dated 1965-10; only the title is quotable). Rejected earlier: Philco 1946 and AT&T Harmon 1962 stylus/light-beam patents (patents, not shown working), 1963 light-pen patent (pointing device, not touch). Gesture and glove side: nothing earlier (Sayre Glove 1977, theremin is an instrument).

name: Speech recognition and voice command
definition: A machine that recognizes spoken words and carries out spoken commands, such as voice-operated doors or computers.
what: Threshold Technology (Delran/Cinnaminson, NJ) brought out the VIP-100 isolated-word recognizer and had voice-input terminals working in industrial, government and military 'real-world' use from late 1972.
fit: Spoken words were recognized by a commercial machine and used to enter data and give commands to a computer in working environments, outside the laboratory.

sources.publisher: Proceedings, 1972 Carahan Conference on Electronic Prosthetics
sources.title: Proceedings, 1972 Carahan Conference on Electronic Prosthetics
sources.quote: A respectable product was brought out this year by Threshold Technology, Inc.

sources.title: Real-time interactive speech technology at Threshold Technology, Incorporated
sources.quote: Threshold Technology has had voice input systems operating in these "real-world" environments since late 1972

note: Replaces the 1984 Apricot Portable. The same ERIC history says 'No commercially successful ASR device of any consequence has been developed in all these years' before Threshold's 1972 product, which supports 1972 as the first; Computerworld 1972-05-31 reports Threshold's lab demonstration of word input. Not checked: the exact first customer installation (1972-73), the earlier IBM Shoebox (1962, demonstration only) and Japanese NEC systems. A 1972 date rests on the 1977 company paper for deployment plus the contemporary product announcement.

name: Speech recognition and voice command
definition: A machine that recognizes spoken words and carries out spoken commands, such as voice-operated doors or computers.
what: Apple launched the iPhone 4S with the Siri voice assistant, putting spoken commands in the hands of ordinary phone users (over four million phones in the launch weekend).
fit: Ordinary people spoke commands and queries to their phones, which recognized the words and carried them out.

sources.title: Digit Magazine November 2011
sources.quote: a faster GPU and Siri - a voice controlled intelligent assistant

sources.title: Siri
sources.quote: On October 14, 2011, Apple launched the iPhone 4S with a beta version of Siri.

note: Kept the second pass. A possibly earlier mass use is AT&T's Voice Recognition Call Processing (1992), where callers say 'collect' or 'person to person' to a machine and which handled more than a billion calls a year; it exists in the AT&T Technology 1994 index but I could not fetch a page with the text (lending books gave 401/403), and callers did not choose it, so I left it out. Dragon NaturallySpeaking (1997) was a niche dictation product.

name: Automatic dictation transcription
definition: A machine that listens to dictation and produces the written or typed text automatically.
what: RCA Laboratories (Harry Olson and Herbert Belar, Princeton) built a phonetic typewriter model that typed spoken sounds; reported in J. Acoust. Soc. Am. in 1956 and confirmed by RCA to the press in August 1956.
fit: A machine listens to speech and types the words automatically, as a single-talker laboratory model with a small vocabulary.

sources.publisher: Journal of the Acoustical Society of America (Crossref record)
sources.title: Phonetic Typewriter
sources.quote: a simplified model of a phonetic typewriter has been developed incorporating all of these aspects

sources.title: The Atlanta Constitution, 2 August 1956
sources.quote: is a phonetic typewriter using an electronic brain to memorize words

sources.title: Challenge August-September 1956
sources.quote: developed a model of such a voice-operated typewriter which is 80 per cent accurate

note: Replaces the second pass (Kyoto Sonotype 1961). Earlier candidates: Steno-Sonograph (Electronics, Sept 1950; fetched) prints visual sound characters for a human stenographer to read and 'is not yet perfected', so no text output, rejected; Typo-Sonograph in the same article was only under construction; Bell Labs 1952 digit recognizer (Audrey) recognizes ten spoken digits, not dictation text. Date 1956-07 is the JASA record date (the abstract appeared in the 1956 volume; full paper Nov 1956); Kyoto 1960-61 and Tangora 1980s are later.

name: Automatic dictation transcription
definition: A machine that listens to dictation and produces the written or typed text automatically.
what: Kurzweil Applied Intelligence officially released its 1,000-word Voicerad system in Boston in December 1986; a radiologist was already writing his reports with it by voice. Dragon Systems had announced Voicescribe-1000 'automatic dictation transcription system' in June 1986.
fit: A computer listens to a user's spoken dictation of reports and produces the edited, printed text, used by a working radiologist.

sources.title: Voice system cures MD ills
sources.quote: allows radiologists to dictate, edit and print out diagnostic X-ray reports by voice

sources.title: Speech transcriber announced
sources.quote: announced Voicescribe-1000, an automatic dictation transcription system

note: Replaces Dragon Dictate 1990 in the second pass: Kurzweil Voicerad and Dragon Voicescribe-1000 were dictation products in 1986 (PC Magazine 27 Oct 1987 also lists both). Earlier: Threshold Technology voice input from 1972 was data entry of commands, not dictation; Kurzweil 1985 Voice Report not found in searches. Voicescribe-1000 was only announced in June 1986 (availability not shown), so Voicerad December 1986 is the first documented in use. Limited vocabulary and discrete speech, so a strict dictation fit but narrow.

name: Speech synthesis
definition: A machine that generates spoken language with an artificial voice, such as a talking computer reading out answers.
what: Texas Instruments' Speak & Spell (introduced June 1978) put a speech-synthesiser chip in a child's hand-held toy; by 1980-81 it was an ordinary household device.
fit: An electronic device generated spoken words with an artificial voice (TMC0280 linear-predictive speech synthesizer) to talk to ordinary users, though only from stored words, not arbitrary text.

sources.title: Implications of Hand Held Electronic Games and Microcomputers for Informal Learning
sources.quote: the gane presents questions and provides feedback with a synthesized voice, a unique application of mi- croelectronic technology in hand held games

sources.title: Speak & Spell (toy)
sources.quote: The first Speak & Spell was introduced at the summer Consumer Electronics Show in 1978

note: Replaces second pass 2011 (Siri). Speak & Spell and talking chess/bridge computers (Popular Electronics ads and reviews 1980) were bought by ordinary families years before Siri; the year is a judgment (introduction 1978, routine household use evident by 1980-81) because no sales figure could be fetched. Strict reading (open-ended text-to-speech, a computer reading out answers) would point to later dates (e.g. Macintosh MacInTalk 1984, Siri 2011); I rejected that because the definition only asks for a machine that generates spoken language.

name: Machine-generated writing
definition: A computer that composes stories, articles, poems or books automatically.
what: ChatGPT, launched 30 Nov 2022, reached 100 million users within about two months, making machine-written text a routine tool for ordinary people.
fit: Ordinary users ask a computer for essays, stories, poems and articles and receive them written automatically.

sources.title: ChatGPT
sources.quote: ChatGPT gained one million users in five days and 100 million in two months.

sources.title: 9th London International Conference 2023
sources.quote: 100 million users two months after it went public in November 2022

note: Date moved from the launch (2022-11-30) to the 100-million-user mark (about 2023-01). Earlier mass writing aids (autocomplete, Smart Compose 2018, GPT-3 apps 2020-21) wrote fragments or were used by few.

name: Machine learning
definition: A machine that improves its performance from experience or data instead of being explicitly programmed for each task.
what: Claude Shannon at Bell Labs built Theseus, a relay-driven magnetic 'mouse' that explored a rearrangeable maze by trial and error and then ran straight to the goal on the next trial (13 s against 2 min 10 s), re-learning when the maze was changed.
fit: A machine improved its performance from experience (its relay memory of the maze it had explored) instead of being programmed with the maze.

sources.title: Shannon and his maze-solving mechanical mouse
sources.quote: The mighty mouse had remembered the maze perfectly!

sources.title: Maze for Mechanical Mouse
sources.quote: After one exploratory trial, the mouse “remembers” exactly how to proceed directly to the goal.

sources.title: Claude Shannon
sources.quote: In 1950, Shannon designed and built, with the help of his wife, Betty, a learning machine named Theseus.

note: Moves the second pass's 1951 (SNARC) back to 1950 (Theseus, built 1950; shown at the 1951 Macy cybernetics conference and in Bell Labs press in 1952). SNARC (Minsky and Edmonds, summer 1951) is later and was reported only on Wikipedia. Other candidates: Ashby's Homeostat 1948 (adapts to disturbances by random search for stability, closer to self-regulation, rejected), Grey Walter's tortoises 1948 (no learning; his conditioned-reflex version is 1951), Samuel's checkers program (1952 running, 1959 paper), Rosenblatt's perceptron 1957-58, Thomas Ross's 1930s maze-solving machine discussed in Psychological Review 1935 (could not read a description in the available text, so not used). Exact month of first demonstration not established.

name: Robot vacuum cleaner and lawn mower
definition: A small autonomous machine that cleans floors or mows a lawn on its own.
what: iRobot's Roomba (debut September 2002) had sold over two million units by late 2006, in millions of homes
fit: A small autonomous floor-cleaning robot used routinely by ordinary households.

sources.title: SERVO Magazine, November 2006
sources.quote: is the run-away best selling "home robot" ever, with over two million sold and counting

note: New kind (the second pass had none). Roomba launched 2002 and was the first commercially successful robot vacuum; 'common' is a judgement, and 2005-2007 is plausible. Trilobite 1996 failed in the market.

name: Service robot for the public
definition: A robot that serves customers or the public as a waiter, bartender, clerk, receptionist or guide.
what: SoftBank's Pepper humanoid was introduced in Tokyo on 5 June 2014 and placed in SoftBank Mobile phone stores in Japan to greet and serve customers.
fit: A robot placed in shops to receive and talk with customers as a greeter/receptionist.

sources.title: Pepper (robot)
sources.quote: showcased in SoftBank Mobile phone stores in Japan beginning the next day

note: This is certainly NOT the earliest: web-search snippets (not fetched, not quotable) report robot waiters Tanbo R-1/R-2 at the Two Panda Deli/Restaurant in Pasadena in 1983 (called the first restaurant with robot waiting staff by Guinness) and Ken-chan at Grazie's, Tokyo, 1985; also the RHINO museum tour-guide robot at Deutsches Museum Bonn, May 1997 (first interactive museum tour-guide). Pages for these (cyberneticzoo, paleofuture, gizmodo, Guinness: proxy blocked; Smithsonian: 403; CMU PDFs: unreachable; archive.org books: lending 401/403) could not be fetched, so I could not source them. Pepper kept only as a sourced reference milestone; a later agent should source Tanbo 1983 as the likely true first practical use.

name: Companion or sex robot
definition: A robot built to provide companionship, affection, romance or sex.
what: Tiger Electronics showed the working Furby, an electronic robotic pet toy that reacts to touch, light and sound and 'learns' to speak, to buyers and press at the American International Toy Fair in New York.
fit: A small motorised, sensor-equipped robot built to act as an affectionate pet-like companion that responds to its owner, which is a loose but real match to a robot built for companionship (no romance or sex function).

sources.publisher: Mary Beth's Beanie World: Furby Edition
sources.title: Mary Beth's Beanie World: Furby Edition
sources.quote: completed the sam- ple Furby just in time for the annual eight day Toy Fair festival held in New York

sources.title: Furby
sources.quote: Furby's first public appearance was at the 1998 American International Toy Fair held in New York City.

note: Replaces second pass 1999-05 (AIBO). Furby (Feb 1998 Toy Fair) is earlier and is a robotic pet toy; I accept it as a companion robot but the fit is loose (a talking, moving toy rather than a sophisticated robot), so low confidence. If Furby is judged only a toy, the next fitting event is Sony's AIBO ERS-110, announced 1999-05-11. Paro was designed from 1993 but first exhibited only in late 2001; Elektro/Sparko 1939 were exhibits; Omnibot (1984) and Teddy Ruxpin (1985) were toy robots/animatronics sold for play, not marketed as companions. RealDoll (1996-97) is a doll, not a robot; no earlier romance or sex robot found.

name: Companion or sex robot
definition: A robot built to provide companionship, affection, romance or sex.
what: Furby went on general sale in the United States (launched 2 October 1998, with a press event at FAO Schwarz, New York), selling 1.8 million in 1998.
fit: The robotic pet toy was bought and kept by ordinary families as a companion that responds to touch and sound.

sources.publisher: Mary Beth's Beanie World: Furby Edition
sources.title: Mary Beth's Beanie World: Furby Edition
sources.quote: for his grand arrival at the flagship FAO Schwarz store in early October

sources.title: Furby
sources.quote: The product officially launched on October 2, 1998

note: Replaces second pass 1999-06-01 (AIBO sale; Sony's robot dog went on sale 1999-06-01, 3,000 units in Japan sold out in 20 minutes per a 1999-06-04 news item) because Furby was on sale eight months earlier. Same fit caveat as the demonstration. Paro handmade sales from 2004 are later.

name: Robot police and security guards
definition: Robots that patrol, guard buildings, check credentials or arrest people on behalf of authorities.
what: Denning Mobile Robotics' Sentry, marketed as an autonomous mobile security robot guard patrolling warehouses; prison units ordered by Southern Steel (600 ordered, 8 in advanced testing in late 1985).
fit: A robot that patrols facilities on its own and alerts authorities to intruders, sold to customers for real guard duty.

sources.title: Raising a new generation of robots
sources.quote: mobile se curity robot guard works in: dependently patrolling warehouses and other facilities

sources.title: Denning Sentry robot article
sources.quote: eight of these, destined for prison duty, are now undergoing ad- vanced testing

note: Replaces 2015 Knightscope: Denning Sentry (1985-86) was earlier. The exact first customer patrol deployment date was not found (1985 sources say testing/orders; Dec 1985 Robotics Age lists it as a product). Date 1986 is the earliest source describing it as working patrol service. RoboGuard/Prowler not checked.

name: Central computer directing many robots
definition: A single computer or master robot that coordinates and directs a whole population of robots.
what: Volvo's Kalmar car plant (Sweden, opened 1974) moved car bodies and engines on a fleet of about 250 battery-powered, computer-guided assembly carriers.
fit: A computer guides a whole fleet of driverless self-moving carriers; the source says only 'computer-guided', so the central-computer coordination is inferred, not quoted.

sources.title: Architecture Plus, November 12, 1974
sources.quote: battery-powered and computer-guided, that creep silently about the factory bearing body assemblies

note: Replaces Kiva 2006/2007 in the second pass, which is too late. Volvo Kalmar (1974) is the earliest dated computer-guided driverless fleet found. Caveat: the fetchable page does not say a single central computer directs the carriers; sources that do say so (Management planning and control systems 1977; Time 1974-11-11; People at Work 1977) are lending-library or did not yield the text, so unverified. Rejected: 1950s Barrett driverless tractors (wire-guided, not computer directed); Tetra Pak Lund 1976 (no fetchable source); Kiva/Walgreens 2007 and Staples 2006 (later).

name: Central computer directing many robots
definition: A single computer or master robot that coordinates and directs a whole population of robots.
what: Volvo Kalmar assembly plant in regular production use of its fleet of computer-guided carriers.
fit: Same event: the carriers did the plant's real production work under computer guidance, but the central-coordination detail is not quoted from a fetched page.

sources.title: Architecture Plus, November 12, 1974
sources.quote: forms of "carriers," battery-powered and computer-guided, that creep silently about the factory bearing body assemblies

note: Same event as the demonstration, so same date. Replaces Walgreens/Kiva 2007. Fit is partial (computer-guided fleet; central control inferred).

name: Machine-readable identity and access card
definition: A card, disc or token encoded with a person's identity that machines read to grant access or check identity.
what: Line Material Industries (McGraw-Edison) used the IBM 357 data collection system in which each employee inserts his identification card at a station, the machine records who he is and his time and attendance.
fit: A machine reads each employee's ID card in daily factory use to identify him and record attendance and production against his name.

sources.title: American Machinist 1961-09-18: Vol 105 Iss 19
sources.quote: Each employee inserts his identification card in the 357 station nearest his job loca- tion

note: The ad of Sept 1961 shows a customer in use; a first use in late 1960 is likely but I found no earlier customer report. The second pass's 1968 RIT VALI-DINE (punched-hole cards admitting students to a dining hall) is later but is the earliest access-control use I found.

name: Automated face recognition
definition: Cameras and computers that identify people by matching their faces against stored images.
what: By 1994 facial-recognition biometric products had reached the marketplace (access control); the DMV offices of West Virginia and New Mexico followed, using automated face recognition against duplicate licences after the 1993 FERET test.
fit: Commercial systems used cameras and computers to match a person's face against an enrolled stored image for entry control and identity checks.

sources.title: Biometric Identification Verification Technology Status and Feasibility Study
sources.quote: Systems which have reached the marketplace include fingerprint, thumbprint, hand geometry, keystroke dynamics, signature dynamics, voice patterns, retina patterns, and facial recognition.

sources.title: Facial recognition system
sources.quote: became the first DMV offices to use automated facial recognition systems to prevent people from obtaining multiple driving licenses

note: Replaces second pass 1997 (ZN-Face sale). The 1994 DTIC study says facial recognition products were already on the market but names no deployment and calls them unreliable (it judged them unable to meet DoD needs), so the date is the earliest documented market presence, not a documented first user. The DMV use (West Virginia, New Mexico) is after 1993 but I found no dated source. Mexico 2000 and Super Bowl 2001 are later.

name: Mind-reading machine
definition: A machine that reads a person's specific thoughts, memories or images directly from their brain.
what: Polyn, Natu, Cohen and Kahana (Univ. of Pennsylvania) used fMRI pattern classifiers to show that the category (faces, locations, objects) of items a person was about to recall could be read from brain activity before the verbal recall.
fit: A machine-learning decoder reads the content category of a person's memory recall directly from brain activity, although only at coarse category level, not specific thoughts or images.

sources.title: Category-Specific Cortical Activity Precedes Retrieval During Memory Search
sources.quote: The reappearance of a given category's activity pattern correlates with verbal recalls made from that category and precedes the recall event by several seconds.

note: Replaces the second pass (ATR/Kyoto 2008 10x10-pixel reconstruction of SEEN images), which is decoding of perception, not of thoughts or memories. Polyn 2005 is the earliest fitting item found: it decodes recalled (remembered) content, though only the category. Considered and rejected: Kamitani and Tong 2005 (decodes seen oriented gratings, perception); Haxby 2001 (seen object categories); Yang Dan 1999 (cat thalamus, animal and seen images); P300 'guilty knowledge' / brain-fingerprinting tests of 1988-91 (EEG detects recognition of a given probe item, not reading unknown content, so a lie-detector rather than a thought reader); Haynes 2007 intention decoding and Horikawa 2013 dream decoding (later); 2025 'mind captioning' of recalled content (later). Borderline fit, hence low.

name: Thought-to-text and thought display
definition: A machine that writes down a person's thoughts as text, or shows their mental images or dreams on a screen.
what: Tomoyasu Horikawa (NTT Communication Science Laboratories) published 'mind captioning': fMRI activity of people recalling videos from memory was decoded into semantic features and turned into free descriptive sentences of the recalled content.
fit: It writes out in sentences, by machine from brain activity alone, what a person is mentally picturing (recalled video content), not what they say or try to say; mechanism is fMRI decoding into language-model features with iterative text generation.

sources.title: Mind captioning: Evolving descriptive text of mental content from human brain activity
sources.quote: The method also generalized to verbalize recalled content, functioning as an interpretive interface between mental representations and text

sources.title: Mind captioning: Evolving descriptive text of mental content from human brain activity
sources.quote: generates descriptive text mirroring brain representations via semantic features computed by a deep language model

note: Replaces the 2020 UCSF result (Makin/Chang), which decodes overt speech from a 50-sentence set and is not thoughts. Rejected candidates: Dewan 1964 alpha-rhythm Morse code and the 1988 P300 speller (letter selection by voluntary attention/blinking, not decoding of thought); Horikawa et al. 2013 (Science) dream decoding and Horikawa & Kamitani 2017 imagined-object decoding (output is predicted object category labels from a fixed list, not text or images of the thoughts); Miyawaki 2008 and Nishimoto 2011 image/movie reconstruction (stimulus the person is seeing, per the test cases); Shen et al. 2019 imagery reconstruction (crude shapes, from fMRI, not text); Tang et al. 2023 (semantic decoder of perceived/imagined speech: speech, excluded by the test case); Moses 2021 and Willett 2021 (attempted speech/handwriting); Kunz 2025 inner speech (imagined speech). Mind captioning 2025 is the earliest I found that turns non-verbal mental content (recalled videos) into free text, and it still needs hours of fMRI training per person, so it is a partial fit; low confidence. Not verified as the first: later work could be argued either way.

name: Brain-computer interface
definition: A link from the brain's electrical signals to a machine, so that a person controls devices by thought alone.
what: Edmond M. Dewan (US Air Force Cambridge Research Laboratories) demonstrated a device that detects the brain's alpha rhythm and let a person send Morse code to a machine by voluntarily switching the rhythm on and off.
fit: Scalp EEG signals are filtered and detected by a machine, and the person sends coded commands to it by voluntary brain activity alone, without moving a muscle.

sources.title: Air Force Research Review 1964-11: Vol 3 Iss 9
sources.quote: Dewan has successfully demonstrated his device to several doctors by operating it with his own alpha rhythm.

note: Replaces Lucier's Music for Solo Performer (1965): later than Dewan's 1964 report, and as an artwork it is borderline (alpha waves of the performer drive percussion via analog amplifiers; I accept it as a borderline BCI but it is not the earliest). Vidal 1973-77 (the 'BCI challenge', VEP cursor/maze) is later; Fetz 1969 monkeys and Grey Walter 1964 not verified or animal. Dewan's exact demonstration date is not given beyond the Nov 1964 report, so the year is the report's year or slightly earlier. Only one contemporary source; the Luce 1966 book 'Sleep' mentions Dewan's alpha filter but is a lending book that cannot be read.

name: Sleep learning
definition: Teaching people while they sleep or are hypnotized by playing recorded lessons.
what: Zust et al. (University of Bern) played recorded pseudoword/German word pairs to young adults in slow-wave sleep and found they had formed and kept new word associations that showed up on an implicit test after waking.
fit: Recorded vocabulary was played to sleeping people and they retained new verbal associations from it, so teaching by recorded sound during sleep worked, though only for implicit word-pair associations and not for general lessons.

sources.title: Implicit Vocabulary Learning during Sleep Is Bound to Slow-Wave Peaks
sources.quote: While in slow-wave sleep during a nap, a series of word pairs comprising pseudowords, e.g., "tofer," and actual German words, e.g., "Haus" (house), were played

note: Second pass gave nothing. This is the earliest strictly fitting result I found. Rejected: Saliger's Psycho-Phone (1927, patented 1932, sold as a sleep-teaching phonograph) and 1950s-60s commercial sleep-learning records, because there was no evidence they worked (the Wikipedia history says Emmons and Simon's 1956 EEG studies found material presented during sleep was not recalled and called it 'impractical and probably impossible'); Arzi et al. 2012 (Nature Neuroscience, 'Humans can learn new information during sleep') showed learning of tone-odour associations in sleep, which is conditioning rather than teaching with lessons, so earlier but a loose analogue; Schreiner and Rasch 2015 only cued words learned while awake. Hypnosis tapes: no controlled evidence found. The abstract itself says earlier evidence 'is inconclusive'. Hence low confidence.
